title: God’s Covenant and Moses’ Commission
overview: Exodus Chapter 6 reveals God's reaffirmation of His covenant promises to the patriarchs and His commitment to deliver Israel from Egyptian bondage. God identifies Himself as the LORD (Jehovah), emphasizing His faithfulness and power to redeem His people. Despite Israel’s despair and Moses’ self-doubt, God commands Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of Egypt. The chapter also provides a genealogical record of Moses and Aaron, grounding their leadership in the tribe of Levi. This chapter is pivotal as it strengthens Israel’s hope by reminding them of God’s unchanging promises and sets the stage for the forthcoming confrontation with Pharaoh.
structure:
**Verses 1-8: Divine Assurance and Covenant Renewal.** God speaks to Moses, declaring His identity as Jehovah and His intention to deliver Israel with a mighty hand, reaffirming the covenant made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

**Verses 9-12: Israel’s Response and Moses’ Hesitation.** Moses conveys God’s message to Israel, but they do not listen due to their suffering. Moses expresses his concern about his ability to persuade Pharaoh.

**Verses 13-27: Genealogy of Moses and Aaron.** The chapter details the lineage of Moses and Aaron, establishing their Levitical heritage and legitimacy as God’s chosen leaders.

**Verses 28-30: Final Commission and Moses’ Continued Doubt.** God reiterates His command to Moses to speak to Pharaoh, while Moses again voices his insecurities about his speaking ability.

keyVerses.text: And God spake unto Moses, and said unto him, I am the LORD:
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's self-identification as the LORD (Jehovah), emphasizing His eternal and covenantal nature. It underscores the authority behind Moses’ mission and God's personal commitment to His people.

keyVerses.text: Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates God's promise of deliverance and redemption, highlighting His power ('stretched out arm') and justice ('great judgments'). It assures Israel of God’s active intervention on their behalf.

keyVerses.text: And I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God: and ye shall know that I am the LORD your God, which bringeth you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
keyVerses.significance: Here God promises a personal relationship with Israel, marking them as His people and Himself as their God. This covenantal relationship is foundational for Israel’s identity and faith.

keyVerses.text: And Moses spake before the LORD, saying, Behold, the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me; how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of uncircumcised lips?
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals Moses’ human weakness and insecurity, highlighting the tension between divine calling and human frailty. It sets the stage for God’s empowerment of Moses.

keyVerses.text: That the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, I am the LORD: speak thou unto Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say unto thee.
keyVerses.significance: God’s repeated self-identification and command to Moses stress the authority and certainty of the mission. It reassures Moses that God’s power will back his words before Pharaoh.

characters.name: God (The LORD / Jehovah)
characters.description: God reveals Himself as the LORD, the covenant-keeping God who promises to deliver Israel from Egypt. He commissions Moses and Aaron to lead His people and reaffirms His covenant with the patriarchs.

characters.name: Moses
characters.description: God’s chosen leader to confront Pharaoh and deliver Israel. In this chapter, Moses struggles with doubt about his ability to speak effectively and fears rejection by both Israel and Pharaoh.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.description: Moses’ brother and co-leader, who is also commissioned by God. Aaron’s genealogy is given to establish his Levitical heritage and his role in the divine mission.

characters.name: The Children of Israel
characters.description: The enslaved people who are the recipients of God’s promise of deliverance. Their initial lack of faith and despair highlight the difficulty of trusting God’s promises amid suffering.

themes.description: This chapter emphasizes God’s unchanging commitment to His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, assuring Israel that He will fulfill His promises despite present hardships.
God promises to redeem Israel from Egyptian bondage with a mighty hand, underscoring His power and justice in liberating His people.
Moses’ repeated doubts about his speaking ability demonstrate human frailty, while God’s reassurance highlights the necessity of divine strength in fulfilling His purposes.
The genealogical record roots Moses and Aaron’s leadership in the tribe of Levi, reinforcing God’s providential preparation and the importance of lineage in Israel’s history.

historicalContext: Exodus 6 is set during the period of Israelite slavery in Egypt, traditionally dated to the Late Bronze Age (circa 15th century BC). Egypt was a dominant regional power with a complex social hierarchy and a polytheistic religion. The Israelites, a distinct ethnic group, lived as slaves under harsh conditions. The political climate was one of oppression, with Pharaoh exercising absolute authority. The covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob concerning the land of Canaan were well known among the Israelites, providing hope amid their suffering. The genealogical details reflect ancient Near Eastern customs of tracing tribal and family lineage to establish authority and identity.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign covenant faithfulness and the assurance that His promises will be fulfilled despite human weakness. Moses’ doubts highlight the necessity of God’s grace and empowerment in the work of redemption.

Dispensationalists see this chapter as a clear distinction between God’s dealings with Israel and the church, focusing on the literal fulfillment of the covenant promises to the patriarchs, including the land inheritance.

Early church interpreters often saw God’s self-revelation as Jehovah as a revelation of the divine name and character, emphasizing God’s holiness and faithfulness. Moses’ hesitation is viewed as a model of humility before God’s calling.

crossReferences.connection: God’s covenant promise to Abraham is reiterated in Exodus 6, showing continuity in God’s plan to bless and deliver His people.
This verse highlights God’s love and faithfulness in choosing Israel, paralleling the covenant reaffirmed in Exodus 6.
The psalm celebrates God’s mighty hand in delivering Israel from Egypt, echoing the promises made in Exodus 6.
Paul references God’s sovereign power over Pharaoh, which aligns with God’s declaration of a 'strong hand' in Exodus 6.
This passage honors Moses’ faith and leadership in delivering Israel, rooted in the commission described in Exodus 6.

application: Trust in God’s faithfulness even when circumstances seem hopeless, remembering His covenant promises.
Recognize that God often uses human weakness to display His power and glory, encouraging humility and dependence on Him.
Embrace your God-given identity and calling, grounded in His providential plan and promises.
Be encouraged to persevere in obedience despite discouragement or opposition, knowing God’s deliverance is certain.
Speak boldly God’s truth, relying on His authority rather than your own abilities.
Remember that God’s relationship with His people is personal and covenantal, inviting us into a deeper knowledge of Him.
conclusion: Exodus 6 stands as a powerful reminder of God’s unwavering covenant faithfulness and His sovereign power to redeem His people. Despite Israel’s suffering and Moses’ doubts, God’s promises remain sure, offering hope and assurance. The chapter’s genealogical details root the divine mission in history and heritage, while the repeated divine self-identification as Jehovah underscores God’s personal commitment. For believers today, this chapter encourages trust in God’s promises, reliance on His strength amid weakness, and faithful obedience to His calling.
